subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Write any two preparations of phenol.

verification.note: Unit 16 (Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.108-112, from the shaded sub-box "ALCOHOLS, PHENOLS AND ETHERS" of printed chapter 12 ("12. ORGANIC CHEMISTRY", a container of four unnumbered sub-boxes each restarting at 1). The book prints this question on book p.111 as Short Answer 8. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK CONTRADICTS ITSELF: this answer prints "623K and 320atms" for the chlorobenzene route, while the same conversion printed as Very Short Answer 5 on book p.109 reads "623K, 300 atm". Two pressures for one reaction. The card writes 300 atm, which is the NCERT value, and records the disagreement. BOOK GAP, added here: the printed diazotisation gives no temperature. A diazonium salt is stable only in the cold, so the diazotisation is carried out at 273-278 K; above that the salt hydrolyses on its own and the yield falls. Leaving the temperature out is a real omission, not a detail. BOOK TYPO: "daizonization" for diazotisation. BALANCE CHECKED, all four equations: C₆H₅Cl + 2NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + NaCl + H₂O (C 6=6, H 7=7, O 2=2, Na 2=2, Cl 1=1); C₆H₅ONa + HCl → C₆H₅OH + NaCl (C 6=6, H 6=6, O 1=1, Na 1=1, Cl 1=1); C₆H₅NH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl → C₆H₅N₂Cl + NaCl + 2H₂O (C 6=6, H 9=9, N 2=2, O 2=2, Na 1=1, Cl 2=2); C₆H₅N₂Cl + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl (C 6=6, H 7=7, N 2=2, O 1=1, Cl 1=1). The book prints only reagents over arrows and balances none of these. TREND AND EXCEPTION: the card states that warming the diazonium salt with water gives the phenol, and names on the same card that this is not automatic — the SAME diazonium salt gives chlorobenzene with Cu₂Cl₂ and HCl, iodobenzene with KI, and benzene with H₃PO₂, so it is the warm water that makes this a preparation of phenol.

steps.label: From chlorobenzene: conditions
lines: Method 1: from chlorobenzene, called
Dow's process.
Chlorobenzene is heated with aqueous NaOH
at 623 K under 300 atm pressure.
Sodium phenoxide is formed, and dilute HCl
then gives phenol.
The severe conditions are needed because
the C–Cl bond of an aryl halide has partial
double bond character and is hard to break.
steps.why: The conditions are the answer here, not a footnote. In an alkyl halide the same substitution happens at room temperature; in an aryl halide the C–Cl bond is shortened and strengthened by resonance, so a temperature of 623 K and a pressure of 300 atm are required. The exception is a ring that already carries strong electron withdrawing groups at positions 2, 4 and 6: 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene gives its phenol with warm water alone.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the temperature and the pressure. Without them this reads like an ordinary substitution, which it is not.
Writing 320 atm, which some books print for this question. The standard value is 300 atm.
steps.memory_tip: Dow's process: chlorobenzene, strong alkali, 623 K, 300 atm.
steps.margin_note: Name the process. A named method is quicker for the examiner to place than a bare set of conditions.

steps.label: From chlorobenzene: equations
lines: Two NaOH are used: one displaces the
chlorine and one neutralises the phenol.
steps.why: The second NaOH is the part most answers miss. Phenol cannot stay as the free acid in a hot alkaline solution, so as soon as it forms it is neutralised, and that consumes a second molecule of alkali. This is also why the acid step is needed at the end.
common_mistakes: Writing one NaOH. Two are consumed, so the equation would not balance.
Showing phenol as the direct product of the alkali step. In alkali the product is the phenoxide.
steps.memory_tip: Two alkalis in, one salt and one water out, then acid to form the phenol.
steps.margin_note: Write both equations, not just the first. The acidification is where the phenol actually appears.

steps.label: From aniline: diazotisation
lines: Method 2: from aniline.
Aniline is treated with NaNO₂ and HCl at
273 to 278 K. This is diazotisation.
The product is benzene diazonium
chloride.
steps.why: The low temperature is part of the method and not a refinement. A diazonium salt is stable only in the cold; above about 278 K it reacts with the water of the solution and the yield of the next step falls. NaNO₂ with HCl supplies the nitrous acid that does the work.
common_mistakes: Omitting the temperature. The book omits it, but a diazotisation written without 273–278 K is incomplete.
Writing HNO₃ instead of NaNO₂ with HCl. Nitric acid would nitrate the ring instead.
steps.memory_tip: Ice cold, nitrous acid made in the flask from NaNO₂ and HCl, and the diazonium salt is used at once.
steps.margin_note: Write the temperature range beside the arrow. It is the one condition an examiner checks in a diazotisation.

steps.label: From aniline: hydrolysis to phenol
lines: The diazonium salt is then warmed with
water.
Nitrogen gas is given off, which is the
visible sign that the reaction is running.
So the two preparations are from
chlorobenzene and from aniline.
steps.why: The nitrogen leaves as a gas, so this step cannot go backwards and the phenol is the final product. It is worth knowing that the warm water is what makes this a phenol preparation: the same diazonium salt gives chlorobenzene with Cu₂Cl₂ and HCl, iodobenzene with KI, and benzene with H₃PO₂.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the nitrogen. Losing N₂ is the whole reason the reaction goes to completion.
Warming the diazonium salt before it is needed. It is made cold and hydrolysed at once, in that order.
steps.memory_tip: Cold to make the diazonium salt, warm water to turn it into phenol, and nitrogen bubbles off.
steps.margin_note: Close with one line naming the two methods. The question asks for two, so say plainly that two have been given.

insider_note: Both routes are common answers, but the two conditions are where marks go: 623 K with 300 atm for the chlorobenzene route, and 273 to 278 K for the diazotisation. Some books omit the diazotisation temperature altogether and print 320 atm in one place against 300 atm in another.
